claim: Down syndrome is the leading genetic cause of intellectual disability.
source: Down syndrome, the leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, results from an extra-copy of chromosome 21.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation in the introduction.

claim: Down syndrome results from an extra-copy of chromosome 21.
source: Down syndrome, the leading genetic cause of intellectual disability, results from an extra-copy of chromosome 21.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about Down syndrome etiology.

claim: Mice engineered to model Down syndrome aneuploidy exhibit Down syndrome-like memory deficits in spatial and contextual tasks.
source: Mice engineered to model this aneuploidy exhibit Down syndrome-like memory deficits in spatial and contextual tasks.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on DS mouse models.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey mice show alterations in the organization of spiking of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Here, using in vivo recording in the Dp(16)1Yey model, we find alterations in the organization of spiking of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, including deficits in the generation of complex spikes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey mice show deficits in the generation of complex spikes in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Here, using in vivo recording in the Dp(16)1Yey model, we find alterations in the organization of spiking of hippocampal CA1 pyramidal neurons, including deficits in the generation of complex spikes.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1J and Figure 3C.

claim: Changes in CA1 pyramidal neuron spiking lead to poorer spatial coding during exploration in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: These changes lead to poorer spatial coding during exploration and less coordinated activity during sharp-wave ripples, events involved in memory consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing larger place fields and decreased spatial information (Figure 1C, D).

claim: Dp(16)1Yey mice show less coordinated activity during sharp-wave ripples.
source: These changes lead to poorer spatial coding during exploration and less coordinated activity during sharp-wave ripples, events involved in memory consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ripple properties and pyramidal cell participation (Figure 4).

claim: Sharp-wave ripples are events involved in memory consolidation.
source: These changes lead to poorer spatial coding during exploration and less coordinated activity during sharp-wave ripples, events involved in memory consolidation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The density of CA1 inhibitory neurons expressing neuropeptide Y is significantly increased in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Further, the density of CA1 inhibitory neurons expressing neuropeptide Y, a population key for the generation of pyramidal cell bursts, were significantly increased in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Neuropeptide Y expressing neurons are a population key for the generation of pyramidal cell bursts.
source: Further, the density of CA1 inhibitory neurons expressing neuropeptide Y, a population key for the generation of pyramidal cell bursts, were significantly increased in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about NPY+ interneuron function, supported by citations.

claim: Down syndrome has an incidence of one in 700 to 1000 live births.
source: Down syndrome (DS), with an incidence of one in 700 to 1000 live births, is the most common genetic cause of intellectual disability (Parker et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Parker et al., 2010.

claim: Down syndrome results from a triplication of chromosome 21 (HSA21).
source: It results from a triplication of chromosome 21 (HSA21) and leads to a wide spectrum of phenotypes, among which craniofacial malformation and intellectual deficits are the most striking for their full penetrance (Antonarakis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Antonarakis et al., 2004.

claim: Craniofacial malformation and intellectual deficits in Down syndrome show full penetrance.
source: It results from a triplication of chromosome 21 (HSA21) and leads to a wide spectrum of phenotypes, among which craniofacial malformation and intellectual deficits are the most striking for their full penetrance (Antonarakis et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Antonarakis et al., 2004.

claim: Behavioral phenotypes in Down syndrome include learning and memory deficits affecting both verbal and non-verbal cognition.
source: The behavioral phenotypes in DS include learning and memory deficits affecting both verbal and non-verbal cognition (Chapman and Hesketh, 2000) and poor performance in spatial memory tasks (Lavenex et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chapman and Hesketh, 2000.

claim: Down syndrome is associated with poor performance in spatial memory tasks.
source: The behavioral phenotypes in DS include learning and memory deficits affecting both verbal and non-verbal cognition (Chapman and Hesketh, 2000) and poor performance in spatial memory tasks (Lavenex et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lavenex et al., 2015.

claim: Cellular defects have been observed in post-mortem brains of Down syndrome fetuses.
source: Cellular defects have been observed in post-mortem brains of DS fetuses (Contestabile et al., 2007; Guidi et al., 2008) but the mechanisms affecting function in the developing and adult DS brain have remained elusive.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Contestabile et al., 2007 and Guidi et al., 2008.

claim: A shift in the balance between inhibitory and excitatory transmission may contribute to Down syndrome learning phenotypes, particularly in the hippocampus.
source: Accumulating data, however, support the idea that a shift in the balance between inhibitory and excitatory transmission may contribute to DS learning phenotypes, particularly in the hippocampus (Kleschevnikov et al., 2012; Kleschevnikov et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kleschevnikov et al., 2012 and 2004.

claim: Targeting alterations in GABAergic signaling may be a viable therapeutic target for Down syndrome.
source: This has led to the proposal that targeting alterations in GABAergic signaling may be a viable therapeutic target (Contestabile et al., 2017), however evidence for this on the circuit level is scarce.
evidence: This is a proposal supported by citation to Contestabile et al., 2017, but noted as lacking circuit-level evidence.

claim: A large portion of HSA21 possesses a syntenic region on mouse chromosome 16 (MMU16).
source: A large portion of HSA21 possesses a syntenic region on mouse chromosome 16 (MMU16), conserving many of the genes in the same order and relative orientation.
evidence: This is established genetic knowledge, also illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mouse models of Down syndrome carrying various lengths of chromosomal duplications recapitulate most of the Down syndrome-like characteristics.
source: These models, carrying various lengths of chromosomal duplications, recapitulate most of the DS-like characteristics (Lana-Elola et al., 2011; Dierssen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lana-Elola et al., 2011 and Dierssen, 2012.

claim: Ts65Dn and Dp(16)1Yey models display learning and memory deficits associated with a loss of hippocampal long-term potentiation.
source: In particular, models carrying some of the largest duplications, Ts65Dn and Dp(16)1Yey, display learning and memory deficits associated with a loss of hippocampal long-term potentiation (Reeves et al., 1995; Kleschevnikov et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Reeves et al., 1995; Kleschevnikov et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2010a.

claim: The transchromosomic Tc1 model carrying a nearly complete HSA21 chromosome shows similar phenotypes to Ts65Dn and Dp(16)1Yey.
source: Similar phenotypes have been described in the transchromosomic Tc1 model carrying a nearly complete HSA21 chromosome (O'Doherty et al., 2005; Morice et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to O'Doherty et al., 2005 and Morice et al., 2008.

claim: Down syndrome mouse models mimic the human condition in regards to hippocampal dependent spatial and working memory deficits.
source: These models thus mimic the human condition in regards to hippocampal dependent spatial and working memory deficits.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion of model phenotypes and citations.

claim: The hippocampus is crucial for the encoding and consolidation of spatial memory in rodents.
source: In rodents the hippocampus is crucial for the encoding and consolidation of spatial memory (Jarrard, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Jarrard, 1993.

claim: CA1 pyramidal neurons exhibit spatial receptive fields referred to as 'place fields'.
source: In the CA1 region pyramidal neurons exhibit spatial receptive fields, referred to as 'place fields', which manifest as discrete locations in the environment where a given cell's firing rate increases (O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to O'Keefe and Dostrovsky, 1971.

claim: During movement the hippocampus exhibits rhythmic population activity in the theta-band (6–12 Hz).
source: Further, during movement the hippocampus exhibits rhythmic population activity in the theta-band (6–12 Hz) which contributes to memory encoding by temporally organizing pyramidal cell spiking (Buzsáki, 2002; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002 and O'Keefe and Recce, 1993.

claim: Theta oscillations contribute to memory encoding by temporally organizing pyramidal cell spiking.
source: Further, during movement the hippocampus exhibits rhythmic population activity in the theta-band (6–12 Hz) which contributes to memory encoding by temporally organizing pyramidal cell spiking (Buzsáki, 2002; O'Keefe and Recce, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Buzsáki, 2002 and O'Keefe and Recce, 1993.

claim: Sharp wave ripples are short high-frequency oscillations (~100 ms, 80–250 Hz) that dominate the hippocampal local field potential during rest or sleep.
source: Following exploration, when animals are resting or sleeping, the hippocampal local field potential is dominated by short high-frequency oscillations (~100 ms, 80–250 Hz) referred to as sharp wave ripples (SWRs; Buzsáki, 2015), events shown to be critical for memory consolidation (Ramadan et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Buzsáki, 2015.

claim: Sharp wave ripples are critical for memory consolidation.
source: Following exploration, when animals are resting or sleeping, the hippocampal local field potential is dominated by short high-frequency oscillations (~100 ms, 80–250 Hz) referred to as sharp wave ripples (SWRs; Buzsáki, 2015), events shown to be critical for memory consolidation (Ramadan et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Ramadan et al., 2009 and Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010.

claim: During sharp wave ripples CA1 pyramidal cells display temporally precise spiking that replays activity related to past behavioral episodes.
source: During SWRs CA1 pyramidal cells display temporally precise spiking that replays activity related to past behavioral episodes (Karlsson and Frank, 2009; Girardeau et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Karlsson and Frank, 2009 and Girardeau et al., 2009.

claim: The precise timing of hippocampal spiking is a crucial feature of creating a functional memory trace during both encoding and consolidation.
source: Thus both during encoding and consolidation the precise timing of hippocampal spiking is a crucial feature of creating a functional memory trace (Buzsáki, 1989).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Buzsáki, 1989.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons regulate the generation of bursts in pyramidal cells.
source: This precision is under the tight control of a diverse family of inhibitory interneurons which regulate the generation of bursts in pyramidal cells, their spike timing within theta during exploratory behavior (Royer et al., 2012) and the synchronization required to generate and maintain ripple events (Pangalos et al., 2013; Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons regulate pyramidal cell spike timing within theta during exploratory behavior.
source: This precision is under the tight control of a diverse family of inhibitory interneurons which regulate the generation of bursts in pyramidal cells, their spike timing within theta during exploratory behavior (Royer et al., 2012) and the synchronization required to generate and maintain ripple events (Pangalos et al., 2013; Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Inhibitory interneurons regulate the synchronization required to generate and maintain ripple events.
source: This precision is under the tight control of a diverse family of inhibitory interneurons which regulate the generation of bursts in pyramidal cells, their spike timing within theta during exploratory behavior (Royer et al., 2012) and the synchronization required to generate and maintain ripple events (Pangalos et al., 2013; Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Pangalos et al., 2013 and Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2013.

claim: Synaptic plasticity deficits have been identified in the hippocampus of Down syndrome mice using in vitro approaches.
source: In vitro approaches have identified synaptic plasticity deficits in the hippocampus of DS mice (Belichenko et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Belichenko et al., 2015.

claim: Long-term potentiation deficits in the dentate gyrus have been observed in vivo in Tc1 mice.
source: Though long-term potentiation deficits in the dentate gyrus (Morice et al., 2008) and mild instability of CA1 place fields (Witton et al., 2015) have been observed in vivo in Tc1 mice, no extensive electrophysiological characterization of a DS mouse model in freely moving conditions has been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Morice et al., 2008.

claim: Mild instability of CA1 place fields has been observed in vivo in Tc1 mice.
source: Though long-term potentiation deficits in the dentate gyrus (Morice et al., 2008) and mild instability of CA1 place fields (Witton et al., 2015) have been observed in vivo in Tc1 mice, no extensive electrophysiological characterization of a DS mouse model in freely moving conditions has been reported.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Witton et al., 2015.

claim: No extensive electrophysiological characterization of a Down syndrome mouse model in freely moving conditions has been reported prior to this study.
source: Though long-term potentiation deficits in the dentate gyrus (Morice et al., 2008) and mild instability of CA1 place fields (Witton et al., 2015) have been observed in vivo in Tc1 mice, no extensive electrophysiological characterization of a DS mouse model in freely moving conditions has been reported.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: The Dp(16)1Yey model carries a large and stable tandem duplication on MMU16.
source: Here we use the Dp(16)1Yey model carrying a large and stable tandem duplication on the MMU16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to circumvent the issue of mosaicism seen in Tc1 mouse brain (~66% chromosome retention in the brain; O'Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tc1 mice show mosaicism with approximately 66% chromosome retention in the brain.
source: Here we use the Dp(16)1Yey model carrying a large and stable tandem duplication on the MMU16 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to circumvent the issue of mosaicism seen in Tc1 mouse brain (~66% chromosome retention in the brain; O'Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to O'Doherty et al., 2005.

claim: There was no difference in average velocity between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice during linear track exploration.
source: We observed no difference between the groups in average velocity (Dp16: 4.17 ± 0.60 cm/s; WT: 4.57 ± 0.19 cm/s; p=0.542) or total distance traveled (Dp16: 4857.92 ± 424.04 cm; WT: 5695.24 ± 318.18 cm; p=0.128).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical comparison.

claim: There was no difference in total distance traveled between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice during linear track exploration.
source: We observed no difference between the groups in average velocity (Dp16: 4.17 ± 0.60 cm/s; WT: 4.57 ± 0.19 cm/s; p=0.542) or total distance traveled (Dp16: 4857.92 ± 424.04 cm; WT: 5695.24 ± 318.18 cm; p=0.128).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data with statistical comparison.

claim: There was no difference in local field potentials between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice across all frequencies during exploration.
source: We first compared local field potentials (LFP) recorded in CA1 while the mice were exploring and found no difference between the groups across all frequencies, including the theta (6–12 Hz) and gamma bands (30–100 Hz) prominent during exploratory behavior (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Place fields in Dp(16)1Yey mice were more diffuse than those in control littermates.
source: Place fields in Dp16 mice were more diffuse than those in their control littermates (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of firing rate maps in Figure 1B and quantitative analysis.

claim: Place fields in Dp(16)1Yey mice were significantly larger than in wild-type mice.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed that in the DS mice the place fields were significantly larger (Figure 1C) and sparser (Firing rate map sparsity: WT: 0.319 ± 0.010; Dp(16)1Yey: 0.359 ± 0.011; p=0.0189), resulting in a significant decrease in the spatial information encoded by these neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Place fields in Dp(16)1Yey mice were sparser than in wild-type mice.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed that in the DS mice the place fields were significantly larger (Figure 1C) and sparser (Firing rate map sparsity: WT: 0.319 ± 0.010; Dp(16)1Yey: 0.359 ± 0.011; p=0.0189), resulting in a significant decrease in the spatial information encoded by these neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis with statistical comparison (p=0.0189).

claim: Spatial information encoded by CA1 pyramidal neurons was significantly decreased in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Quantitative analysis confirmed that in the DS mice the place fields were significantly larger (Figure 1C) and sparser (Firing rate map sparsity: WT: 0.319 ± 0.010; Dp(16)1Yey: 0.359 ± 0.011; p=0.0189), resulting in a significant decrease in the spatial information encoded by these neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The directionality index of pyramidal cells in Dp(16)1Yey mice was comparable to that of wild-type littermates.
source: The 'directionality index' of pyramidal cells in Dp(16)1Yey samples was comparable to that of their WT littermates suggesting that this aspect of coding was conserved (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells from Dp(16)1Yey animals had a significantly lower peak firing rate during exploration.
source: CA1 pyramidal cells from Dp16 animals had a significantly lower peak firing rate during exploration (Figure 1F) but an average firing rate comparable to control littermates (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: CA1 pyramidal cells from Dp(16)1Yey animals had an average firing rate comparable to control littermates during exploration.
source: CA1 pyramidal cells from Dp16 animals had a significantly lower peak firing rate during exploration (Figure 1F) but an average firing rate comparable to control littermates (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey place cells displayed a significantly lower in-field firing rate.
source: On a finer level we observed that Dp16 place cells displayed a significantly lower in-field firing rate but fired normally outside of their place field (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey place cells fired normally outside of their place field.
source: On a finer level we observed that Dp16 place cells displayed a significantly lower in-field firing rate but fired normally outside of their place field (Figure 1H,I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: The complex spike index was drastically lower in Dp(16)1Yey mice compared to controls during exploration.
source: To investigate if the decrease in peak firing rate we observed reflected a loss of the ability to produce the complex spike bursts typical of pyramidal cells we compared the complex spike index (CSI; McHugh et al., 1996) between the groups and found it to be drastically lower in the Dp16 mice (Figure 1J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1J.

claim: The proportion of significantly theta-modulated cells was not significantly different between Dp(16)1Yey and control mice.
source: The proportion of significantly theta-modulated cells was not significantly different between Dp16 and control mice (WT: 121/256, 47.3%; Dp16: 115/259, 44.4%, Chi-square test p=0.514) and the firing probability of significantly theta-modulated CA1 place cells as a function of theta phase showed a highly similar pattern between the groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison (p=0.514).

claim: The firing probability of significantly theta-modulated CA1 place cells as a function of theta phase showed a highly similar pattern between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type groups.
source: The proportion of significantly theta-modulated cells was not significantly different between Dp16 and control mice (WT: 121/256, 47.3%; Dp16: 115/259, 44.4%, Chi-square test p=0.514) and the firing probability of significantly theta-modulated CA1 place cells as a function of theta phase showed a highly similar pattern between the groups (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The preferred phase of theta was similar between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type groups.
source: The preferred phase of theta (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and the concentration of the firing probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; Siapas et al., 2005) were also similar between the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The concentration of the firing probability was similar between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type groups.
source: The preferred phase of theta (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C) and the concentration of the firing probability (Figure 1—figure supplement 2D; Siapas et al., 2005) were also similar between the groups.
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Theta-modulation was unaltered in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Overall, these results indicate that theta-modulation was unaltered in the Dp16 mice.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple measures of theta modulation showing no differences.

claim: The correlation between population vectors decreased rapidly as a function of distance from the diagonal in both control and Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: In both the control (Figure 2A) and Dp16 mice (Figure 2B) the correlation decreased rapidly as a function of distance from the diagonal.
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of autocorrelation matrices in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: There were no significant differences in population vector correlation as a function of distance between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice, except for largely distant population vectors.
source: The averaged values of the correlation between population vectors as a function of distance confirmed this pattern, with no significant differences between the groups, except for largely distant population vectors for which the correlation was lower in the Dp16 animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Control mice showed a clear diagonal band of structure in population vector correlation for laps in opposite directions.
source: Interestingly, whereas there was a clear diagonal band of structure obvious in the control data (Figure 2A), this was not present in the Dp16 data (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of autocorrelation matrices in Figure 2A.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey mice did not show a diagonal band of structure in population vector correlation for laps in opposite directions.
source: Interestingly, whereas there was a clear diagonal band of structure obvious in the control data (Figure 2A), this was not present in the Dp16 data (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by visual inspection of autocorrelation matrices in Figure 2B.

claim: Control mice showed a significant central peak in correlation between population vectors for laps in opposite directions.
source: In control mice the averaged values of the correlation between population vectors as a function of distance showed a significant central peak, with the maximal value slightly shifted to the left (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The shift in the central peak of population vector correlation in control mice may reflect prospective coding of future locations.
source: These findings are similar to previous reports and this shift has been suggested to reflect prospective coding of future locations (Resnik et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on citation to Resnik et al., 2012 and is speculative.

claim: Dp(16)1Yey population vectors failed to show a central peak in correlation for laps in opposite directions.
source: The Dp16 population vectors however failed to show this central peak and correlation values remained significantly lower than in WT mice, even for similar positions on the track.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Direction dependent representation of position is not significantly altered in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that while the direction dependent representation of position is not significantly altered in Dp(16)1Yey mice, the direction independent coding of position observed in control mice is greatly decreased.
evidence: This is inferred from the population vector analysis showing preserved same-direction correlation.

claim: Direction independent coding of position is greatly decreased in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Taken together, these data suggest that while the direction dependent representation of position is not significantly altered in Dp(16)1Yey mice, the direction independent coding of position observed in control mice is greatly decreased.
evidence: This is inferred from the population vector analysis showing loss of opposite-direction correlation.

claim: The peak and average firing rate of CA1 pyramidal cells during post-run rest were not significantly different between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice.
source: During this quiescent period the peak and average firing rate of CA1 pyramidal cells were not significantly different between Dp16 and WT mice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: The complex spiking index was significantly lower in Dp(16)1Yey mice during post-run rest.
source: However, similar to what we observed during exploration, the complex spiking index was significantly lower in the DS model mice, suggesting that the deficit in the generation of complex spikes could impact off-line memory consolidation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The ISI distribution of wild-type pyramidal cells showed a clear narrow peak at short ISIs (~2 to 15 ms) and a second wide peak at longer ISIs (≥100 ms).
source: Plotting the inter-spike interval (ISI) distribution of all spike trains from WT pyramidal cells revealed a clear narrow peak at short ISIs (~2 to 15 ms) and a second wide peak at longer ISIs (≥100 ms; Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ISI distribution of Dp(16)1Yey pyramidal cells showed a reduction of the short ISI peak and a slight increase at longer ISIs.
source: In contrast, the ISI distribution of spike trains recorded from Dp16 pyramidal cells showed a reduction of the short ISI peak and a slight increase at longer ISIs (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The ISI mode was significantly longer in Dp(16)1Yey data compared to controls during rest.
source: Accordingly, the ISI mode, defined as the most frequent ISI for a given cell, was significantly longer in the Dp16 data compared to controls (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Spikes generated by CA1 pyramidal cells in Dp(16)1Yey mice were sparser and less likely to be involved in bursts.
source: An increase in the ISI mode, which preferentially reflects the frequent short ISIs generate by bursts, without a significant change in the mean firing rate suggested that spikes generated by CA1 pyramidal cells in Dp16 mice were sparser and less likely to be involved in bursts.
evidence: This is inferred from the ISI mode increase without mean firing rate change.

claim: The ability of pyramidal cells to fire bursts of spikes is impaired in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Overall, these data indicate that in Dp(16)1Yey mice the ability of pyramidal cells to fire bursts of spikes is impaired.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple measures of bursting showing deficits.

claim: The number of ripples per minute was not significantly different between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice.
source: The number of ripples per minute and mean inter-ripple intervals were not significantly different between Dp16 and WT mice (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mean inter-ripple intervals were not significantly different between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice.
source: The number of ripples per minute and mean inter-ripple intervals were not significantly different between Dp16 and WT mice (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was no significant difference in the peak ripple frequency between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice.
source: Although there was a slight shift in the population distribution towards lower intrinsic frequencies in the DS mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), we found no significant difference in the peak ripple frequency (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Ripples in Dp(16)1Yey mice were significantly smaller in amplitude than those in controls.
source: However ripples in the Dp16 mice were significantly smaller in amplitude (Figure 4E) and shorter in duration than those found in controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Ripples in Dp(16)1Yey mice were significantly shorter in duration than those in controls.
source: However ripples in the Dp16 mice were significantly smaller in amplitude (Figure 4E) and shorter in duration than those found in controls (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The average number of spikes per cell per ripple was slightly yet significantly lower in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: The average number of spikes per cell per ripple was slightly, yet significantly, lower in Dp16 mice (Figure 4G) and pyramidal cells participated in a significantly lower proportion of ripple events (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Pyramidal cells participated in a significantly lower proportion of ripple events in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: The average number of spikes per cell per ripple was slightly, yet significantly, lower in Dp16 mice (Figure 4G) and pyramidal cells participated in a significantly lower proportion of ripple events (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4H.

claim: There was a significant shift toward lower ripple participation rates in Dp(16)1Yey mice, with a peak at 5–10% compared to 10–15% in wild-type mice.
source: Further, plotting the populations of cells according to their ripple participation rates illustrated a significant shift toward lower values in the DS model, with a peak at 5–10% in the Dp16 mice compared to a peak at 10–15% in the WT group (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Changes in single unit activity during ripples were unrelated to the decrease in ripple amplitude in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: These changes in single unit activity were unrelated to the decrease in ripple amplitude in the Dp16 mice, as we found significant decreases in ripple-related spiking and event participation across a wide range of ripple detection thresholds (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis using different detection thresholds shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The density of NPY positive neurons was significantly increased in the stratum pyramidale and stratum lacunosum moleculare layers of Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: The density of these NPY positive neurons was significantly increased in the SP and SLM layers from Dp16 samples (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: No significant differences in NPY positive neuron density were observed in the stratum oriens and stratum radiatum layers between Dp(16)1Yey and wild-type mice.
source: However, no significant differences were observed in the SO and SR layers.
evidence: This is stated based on immunohistochemistry analysis.

claim: The density of PV positive cells was slightly yet significantly decreased in the stratum oriens layer of Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: The density of PV positive cells was slightly yet significantly decreased in the SO layer of the DS mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PV cell density in the stratum pyramidale of Dp(16)1Yey mice trended higher but did not reach the level of significance.
source: In the SP of Dp16 mice PV cell density trended higher, but did not reach the level of significance (Mann-Whitney U-test, p=0.164).
evidence: This is stated based on statistical analysis (p=0.164).

claim: The density of SST positive cells was not significantly different between wild-type and Dp(16)1Yey samples in all four layers of CA1.
source: The density of SST positive cells was not significantly different between WT and Dp16 samples in all four layers of CA1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Dp(16)1Yey model reproduces learning and memory deficits that resemble those seen in people with Down syndrome.
source: The Dp(16)1Yey model for DS reproduces learning and memory deficits that resemble those seen in people with DS.
evidence: This is stated based on prior behavioral and electrophysiological studies cited.

claim: Behavioral screening and in vitro electrophysiology approaches have identified spatial learning and memory deficits associated with long-term potentiation decrease at the Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Behavioral screening and in vitro electrophysiology approaches have identified spatial learning and memory deficits associated with a clear long-term potentiation decrease at the Schaffer collateral-CA1 synapses (Yu et al., 2010a; Yu et al., 2010b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yu et al., 2010a and 2010b.

claim: Pharmacological or genetic abolition of NMDA-based plasticity results in more diffuse place fields and more variability in firing.
source: Pharmacological or genetic abolition of NMDA-based plasticity results in more diffuse place fields and more variability in firing both within and across exploration sessions (Kentros et al., 1998; McHugh et al., 1996; Cabral et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kentros et al., 1998; McHugh et al., 1996; Cabral et al., 2014.

claim: More diffuse place fields in Dp(16)1Yey mice could be a consequence of abnormal synaptic plasticity in the CA1 or upstream trisynaptic circuit.
source: Here we found that place cells of Dp(16)1Yey mice have larger, more diffuse place fields that could be a consequence of abnormal synaptic plasticity, not solely in the CA1, but potentially also in the upstream trisynaptic circuit, as observed in the Tc1 mice (Witton et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data and citation to Witton et al., 2015.

claim: Changes in ripple characteristics in Dp(16)1Yey mice have not been observed in models of chemically induced LTP blockade.
source: Although LTP during exploratory behavior is important for the memory reactivation during ripple events, none of the changes we found in ripple characteristics have been observed in models of chemically induced LTP blockade (Dupret et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated based on comparison with citation to Dupret et al., 2010.

claim: The deficit in bursting and complex spiking in Dp(16)1Yey mice is likely to have a different origin than LTP deficits.
source: These changes, as well as the deficit in bursting and complex spiking, are thus likely to have a different origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison with LTP blockade models.

claim: Deficient pyramidal cell recruitment during ripple events suggests that memory consolidation may be poorer in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: The fact that pyramidal cells recruitment during ripple events is deficient suggests that memory consolidation may be poorer in Dp16 mice and is potentially a key contributor to their learning and memory deficits (Ramadan et al., 2009; Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the data and citations to Ramadan et al., 2009 and Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010.

claim: Basket cells play an important role in maintaining network oscillations and synchronizing pyramidal cells to these rhythms.
source: Basket cells, the dominant PV+/NPY-/SST- fast-spiking class of interneurons, play an important role in maintaining network oscillations and synchronizing pyramidal cells to these rhythms (Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2013; Bartley et al., 2015; Schlingloff et al., 2014; Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: An increase in PV expressing cells has been reported in juvenile Down syndrome mice.
source: Although an increase in PV expressing cells has been reported in juvenile DS mice (Chakrabarti et al., 2010), our results, as well as data from other groups (Hernández-González et al., 2015), do not support this observation in adults.
evidence: This is stated based on citation to Chakrabarti et al., 2010, but contradicted by current and other data.

claim: The current study and data from other groups do not support an increase in PV expressing cells in adult Down syndrome mice.
source: Although an increase in PV expressing cells has been reported in juvenile DS mice (Chakrabarti et al., 2010), our results, as well as data from other groups (Hernández-González et al., 2015), do not support this observation in adults.
evidence: This is based on the current study's data and citation to Hernández-González et al., 2015.

claim: Gamma and theta power, the frequency of ripple events, and the phase locking of pyramidal cells to theta are conserved in the Dp(16)1Yey model.
source: Moreover, we did not see physiological differences between Dp(16)1Yey and control mice that would be predicted by changes in basket cells: gamma and theta power, the frequency of ripple events and the phase locking of pyramidal cells to theta are conserved in the Dp16 model.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The decrease in gamma power observed in vitro under tetanic stimulation in the Ts65Dn model was absent in the Dp(16)1Yey mice under in vivo physiological conditions.
source: The decrease in gamma power observed in vitro under tetanic stimulation in the Ts65Dn model (Hanson et al., 2013) was also absent in the Dp(16)1Yey mice under in vivo physiological conditions.
evidence: This is based on comparison of current data with citation to Hanson et al., 2013.

claim: Oriens-lacunosum moleculare (OLM) cells regulate pyramidal cells' excitability by directly targeting their dendritic tufts.
source: They also express PV weakly and are likely to be NPY positive (Somogyi and Klausberger, 2005; Milstein et al., 2015). These neurons regulate pyramidal cells' excitability by directly targeting their dendritic tufts, affecting pyramidal cells bursts and, unlike basket cells, have no effect on the spike timing (Pangalos et al., 2013; Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Pangalos et al., 2013 and Royer et al., 2012.

claim: OLM cells affect pyramidal cell bursts but have no effect on spike timing.
source: These neurons regulate pyramidal cells' excitability by directly targeting their dendritic tufts, affecting pyramidal cells bursts and, unlike basket cells, have no effect on the spike timing (Pangalos et al., 2013; Royer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Pangalos et al., 2013 and Royer et al., 2012.

claim: Functional changes at the cellular level in OLM interneurons could contribute to the decrease in bursts from pyramidal cells in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: While we did not find a significant alteration in the size of the OLM interneuron population, functional changes at the cellular level in these neurons could contribute to the drastic decrease in bursts from pyramidal cells in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the lack of population changes but presence of functional deficits.

claim: Bistratified cells and Ivy cells are able to directly control pyramidal cells' excitability by affecting the processing of input from the CA3.
source: Both BS and Ivy interneurons are able to directly control pyramidal cells' excitability by affecting the processing of input from the CA3 (Lovett-Barron et al., 2012; Fuentealba et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lovett-Barron et al., 2012 and Fuentealba et al., 2008.

claim: Bistratified cells are known to control the bursting of pyramidal cells and to switch their firing between single spikes and bursts.
source: Though it is not clear if Ivy cells are able to induce a similar effect, BS cells are known to control the bursting of pyramidal cells and to switch their firing between single spikes and bursts (Lovett-Barron et al., 2012; Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to Lovett-Barron et al., 2012 and Cutsuridis and Taxidis, 2012.

claim: The shift in the biphasic distribution of single versus burst spikes in Dp(16)1Yey mice may be caused by enhanced inhibition from bistratified and/or Ivy cells.
source: The shift observed in the biphasic distribution of single versus burst spikes may be caused by an enhanced inhibition from BS and/or Ivy cells.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the increased NPY+ cell density and functional deficits.

claim: A similar increase in NPY positive interneurons at the SLM-SR border has been reported in the Ts65Dn model.
source: In addition, the increased population of NPY positive interneurons at the SLM-SR border corresponds to a recently identified class of interneurons with unique characteristics (Milstein et al., 2015). A similar increase has been reported in the Ts65Dn model (Hernández-González et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Hernández-González et al., 2015.

claim: NPY positive cells at the SLM-SR border are able to integrate inputs from both the CA3 and the entorhinal cortex to trigger complex spikes in pyramidal cells.
source: Unlike PV and SST expressing interneurons, these NPY positive cells are able to integrate inputs from both the CA3 and the entorhinal cortex to trigger complex spikes in pyramidal cells (Milstein et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation to Milstein et al., 2015.

claim: Enhanced inhibition resulting from increased NPY+ interneuron density is likely to impact pyramidal cells in the Dp(16)1Yey model and contribute to the decrease in complex spiking.
source: Enhanced inhibition resulting from increased NPY +interneurons density is thus likely to impact pyramidal cells in the Dp(16)1Yey model and contribute to the decrease in complex spiking seen in these mice.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased NPY+ cell density and the observed decrease in complex spiking.

claim: Deficits in hippocampal plasticity and hippocampal dependent learning and memory are consistent phenotypes in the main mouse models for Down syndrome.
source: Deficits in hippocampal plasticity and hippocampal dependent learning and memory are consistent phenotypes observed not only in this model, but also in the other three main mouse models for DS: Ts1Cje, Ts65Dn and Tc1 (Reeves et al., 1995; Sago et al., 1998; Siarey et al., 1997; Siarey et al., 2005; Belichenko et al., 2007; O'Doherty et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies on different DS mouse models.

claim: The main hypothesis for brain phenotypes in Down syndrome is over-inhibition by the GABAergic system.
source: Over the past decade the extensive study of these DS mice, especially the Ts65Dn model, has led to a main hypothesis that the leading cause for brain phenotypes in DS is over-inhibition by the GABAergic system (Contestabile et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis supported by citation to Contestabile et al., 2017.

claim: The GABAergic over-inhibition hypothesis is based on histological and electrophysiological observations showing increases in interneurons, changes in inhibitory synapse distribution, and increased GABA induced inhibitory currents.
source: This theory is originally based on histological and electrophysiological observations showing increases in interneurons, changes in the repartition of inhibitory synapses, and increased GABA induced inhibitory currents (Chakrabarti et al., 2010; Hernández-González et al., 2015; Belichenko et al., 2004; Belichenko et al., 2009; Best et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to studies showing these observations.

claim: Pharmacological approaches show a rescue of learning, memory and LTP deficits in Down syndrome mice using drugs that decrease inhibitory signaling.
source: It is also supported by pharmacological approaches showing a rescue of the learning, memory and LTP deficits using drugs inducing a decrease in inhibitory signaling (Fernandez et al., 2007; Braudeau et al., 2011; Martínez-Cué et al., 2013; Kleschevnikov et al., 2012; Deidda et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to pharmacological rescue studies.

claim: The GABAergic hypothesis is a leading target for recent clinical trials using broad GABA antagonist compounds.
source: As no drug is available to date for treating Down syndrome phenotypes, the GABAergic hypothesis is a leading target for recent clinical trials using broad GABA antagonist compounds.
evidence: This is stated as current clinical practice based on the hypothesis.

claim: This work provides the first extensive characterization of in vivo neuronal activity in freely behaving Down syndrome model animals.
source: Our work provides the first extensive characterization of the in vivo neuronal activity in freely behaving animals and can serve as the basis for the design of novel biomarkers to address the GABAergic theory in vivo.
evidence: This is stated as a contribution of the current study.

claim: Changes in a limited class of interneurons could support abnormal neuronal function at the circuit level in Down syndrome.
source: Our data indicate that changes occurring in a limited class of interneurons could support abnormal neuronal function at the circuit level, suggesting that drugs targeted to these neurons could prove more successful in treating Down syndrome phenotypes than non-specific GABA antagonists.
evidence: This is inferred from the specific increase in NPY+ interneurons and the functional deficits observed.

claim: Drugs targeted to specific interneuron classes could prove more successful in treating Down syndrome phenotypes than non-specific GABA antagonists.
source: Our data indicate that changes occurring in a limited class of interneurons could support abnormal neuronal function at the circuit level, suggesting that drugs targeted to these neurons could prove more successful in treating Down syndrome phenotypes than non-specific GABA antagonists.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the findings of specific interneuron changes.

claim: The pool of specific inhibitory neurons is increased in the hippocampus of Down syndrome animals.
source: Our data supports previous reports suggesting that the pool of specific inhibitory neurons is increased in the hippocampus of DS animals (Hernández-González et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on the current study's data and citation to Hernández-González et al., 2015.

claim: Very few genes within the trisomic region of Dp(16)1Yey mice are known to have a direct impact on interneuron differentiation.
source: Very few genes within the trisomic region of Dp(16)1Yey mice are known to have a direct impact on interneuron differentiation.
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge about the genetic mechanisms.

claim: Decreased response to SHH signaling, likely through overexpression of App, is a candidate mechanism for interneuron changes in Down syndrome mice.
source: The main candidate mechanisms so far are a decreased response to SHH signaling, most likely though the overexpression of App (Roper et al., 2006; Trazzi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2010) and the direct regulation of embryonic neuronal differentiation by Olig1 and Olig2 in the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE; Chakrabarti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citations to Roper et al., 2006; Trazzi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2010.

claim: Direct regulation of embryonic neuronal differentiation by Olig1 and Olig2 in the medial ganglionic eminence is a candidate mechanism for interneuron changes in Down syndrome mice.
source: The main candidate mechanisms so far are a decreased response to SHH signaling, most likely though the overexpression of App (Roper et al., 2006; Trazzi et al., 2011; Xu et al., 2010) and the direct regulation of embryonic neuronal differentiation by Olig1 and Olig2 in the medial ganglionic eminence (MGE; Chakrabarti et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on citation to Chakrabarti et al., 2010.

claim: An abnormal MGE neuron differentiation mechanism could be responsible for the NPY positive population increase in Dp(16)1Yey mice.
source: Interestingly, although the changes observed by these authors in early post-natal hippocampus are not reproduced at adult stages (Hernández-González et al., 2015), present study), an abnormal MGE neuron differentiation mechanism could be responsible for the NPY positive populations increase in the Dp(16)1Yey mice, as these cells derive from this embryonic structure (Tricoire et al., 2010).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the developmental origin of NPY+ cells and citation to Tricoire et al., 2010.

claim: Dyrk1a is among the top candidate genes for affecting neuronal precursor cell cycle in Down syndrome.
source: The serine-threonine kinase Dyrk1a is also among the top candidates for its ability to affect the neuronal precursors cell cycle, directly or through a synergistic effect with the regulator of calcineurin Rcan1 (Arron et al., 2006; Hämmerle et al., 2011).
evidence: This is based on citations to Arron et al., 2006 and Hämmerle et al., 2011.

claim: The number of bursts per minute was significantly decreased in Dp(16)1Yey mice during both exploration and rest.
source: The number of bursts per minute was significantly decreased in the Dp16 group, whereas the mean inter-burst interval was significantly increased, both during exploration and rest.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The mean inter-burst interval was significantly increased in Dp(16)1Yey mice during both exploration and rest.
source: The number of bursts per minute was significantly decreased in the Dp16 group, whereas the mean inter-burst interval was significantly increased, both during exploration and rest.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Average burst duration was significantly longer in Dp(16)1Yey mice during exploration.
source: Average burst duration was significantly longer in DS mice during exploration, but this was not the case during rest.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The percentage of spikes participating in bursts was significantly lower in Dp(16)1Yey place cells during both memory encoding and consolidation.
source: Moreover, the percentage of spikes participating in bursts, as well as the average number of spikes per burst, were significantly lower in Dp16 place cells, both during memory encoding and consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The average number of spikes per burst was significantly lower in Dp(16)1Yey place cells during both memory encoding and consolidation.
source: Moreover, the percentage of spikes participating in bursts, as well as the average number of spikes per burst, were significantly lower in Dp16 place cells, both during memory encoding and consolidation.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: The decrease in complex spiking index is likely explained by an overall loss of firing during bursts on the single cell level, impacting both encoding and consolidation of spatial information.
source: These findings indicate that the decrease in complex spiking index observed is likely explained by an overall loss of firing during bursts on the single cell level, impacting both the encoding and consolidation of spatial information.
evidence: This is inferred from the multiple measures of bursting deficits.

claim: The Dp(16)1Yey carries a 22.4 Mb tandem duplication spanning from Lipi to Zfp295 on MMU16.
source: The Dp(16)1Yey carries a tandem duplication for the entire region of synteny on MMU16 spanning from Lipi to Zfp295 (~98 known protein coding genes). This 22.4 Mb duplication was obtained by Cre-loxP mediated chromosomal engineering.
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The Dp(16)1Yey duplication includes approximately 98 known protein coding genes.
source: The Dp(16)1Yey carries a tandem duplication for the entire region of synteny on MMU16 spanning from Lipi to Zfp295 (~98 known protein coding genes).
evidence: This is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.
